title:
Joromi and the
Spirit Wrestlers
description: A champion enters the spirit world and discovers that courage and pride are not the same.

source.adaptation: Original Hypa retelling following the escape variant documented by John Collins from Victor Uwaifo. Boxing opponents and patterns are a separate game adaptation; see SOURCES.md.

game.intro: Stay in one spot. Use gentle punches. Guard the glowing side, duck the high sweep, then punch the faces.
game.flat: Stay in one spot. Hold the left or right side of the screen to guard (or A and D), hold low to duck the high sweep (or S), then tap the glowing face to punch (or Space).
game.adaptation: A boxing game inspired by the wrestling tale.
game.recover: Hands back. Watch the next pattern.
game.won: Practice complete. Knowing when to stop is strength.
game.lost: Take a breath. Try this spirit again.

lines.text: Long ago, in the land of the Edo people, a young wrestler named Joromi became famous for his strength.
When he entered the village square, everyone wanted to watch.
He was quick on his feet. He could feel an opponent shift his weight and know which way the next struggle would turn.
One wrestler after another fell before him.
At first, Joromi thanked the people who cheered. But with every victory his pride grew.
Soon he began to believe that there was no one, anywhere, who could defeat him.
His sister knew his courage. She also knew how little he liked a warning.
When she spoke of limits, he heard only a challenge waiting to be answered.
Near their home stood a palm tree that he had been warned not to climb.
To Joromi, even that warning began to sound like an insult to his strength.
One day he grasped the trunk and climbed. His sister called after him.
He kept going, higher than the roofs, higher than the familiar sounds of the village.
ask: Why does his sister warn him?

lines.text: Then the tree carried him beyond the world he knew.
Below him lay the land of people. Before him opened another place, where spirits gathered to wrestle.
Joromi looked at their arena. He had beaten the champions of the human world.
Why should he turn back now? He stepped forward and offered his challenge.
His sister would not abandon him.
In this telling, she changed into a small fly and followed him, carrying her voice where her human feet could not go.
ask: How does his sister help him?

lines.text: The spirits watched the stranger.
Here was a man of flesh and breath, standing in a place that was not his own, asking to prove himself against them.
A spirit with two heads came forward. Joromi met it in the arena.
They strained against one another, neither willing to yield, while the watchers crowded close.
The struggle lasted far longer than any contest Joromi had known at home.
Strength alone was not enough. He had to watch, wait, and find the moment to act.
ask: Why is patience useful in a fight?

lines.text: His sister's voice reached him through the noise. She called his name and reminded him how far he had come.
But each victory also carried him farther from safety.
At last Joromi overcame that opponent. The arena stirred.
He had proved that a human could stand against a spirit. Yet he still did not think of returning home.
Another challenge followed. Now the danger before him was greater.
A terrible spirit with seven heads stood ready to fight, and the air around it seemed to burn.
For the first time, Joromi felt how tired his body had become. His arms were heavy.
His breathing was short. Courage had brought him here; pride had kept him here.
ask: What changes when Joromi becomes tired?

lines.text: Still he fought. The spirit pressed him hard, giving him little time to recover.
His sister stayed close, her small voice refusing to disappear in the confusion.
Joromi struggled free and found a chance to escape.
This was no ordinary village contest, with friends waiting to lift him to their shoulders when it was over.
He turned toward the way home. Down he raced from the spirit world, leaving its champions behind.
The familiar earth beneath his feet was more precious than another victory.
ask: Why does Joromi decide to escape?

lines.text: His sister returned with him. He had entered that strange arena certain that strength could answer every question.
He came back knowing that there were questions strength could not answer.
That is the Joromi remembered in this telling: brave enough to face a frightening opponent,
but brought close to disaster by the wish to defeat everyone.
And when the elder finishes, he leaves a question beside the fire.
Is the strongest person always the one who keeps fighting, or can strength also mean knowing when to stop?
ask: Can knowing when to stop be a kind of strength?
